c.tagline: Sacred rooftop of the world, where the Potala Palace crowns a 3,650-meter Tibetan Buddhist capital.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered starting around 10 RMB, but drivers sometimes bargain a flat fare with tourists instead; having your destination written in Chinese characters helps a lot.

emergency.note: English support is limited; ask your hotel or registered tour guide (required for foreign travel in Tibet) to assist with emergencies and altitude sickness.

avoid.reason: Tibet requires a permit and an organised tour — independent travel is not allowed; politically sensitive, avoid discussing politics

hood_desc: The spiritual heart of Lhasa, centered on the Jokhang Temple and the Barkhor pilgrim circuit lined with stalls, teahouses and pilgrims spinning prayer wheels. Narrow Tibetan-style lanes make it the most atmospheric place to stay.

Home to the towering Potala Palace, the former winter residence of the Dalai Lamas and Lhasa's most iconic landmark. The area around it is more modern and spread out, with wide boulevards and photo-viewpoint parks.
A quieter, leafy district built around the Dalai Lamas' former summer palace and gardens, popular for peaceful strolls away from the old town crowds.
Set at the base of the hills north of the city, this area centers on one of Tibet's great monastic universities, famous for its afternoon monk debates; it has a calm, semi-rural feel.
The modern administrative and commercial core of Lhasa, with shopping malls, chain restaurants and government buildings, offering easy access to services but little historic charm.

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water only, as throughout China.

transit.pay: Cash or QR code (WeChat Pay/Alipay); foreign cards generally not usable
transit.map: Limited English signage on buses; ask your hotel or guide for route help
transit.note: Public transit is limited for foreign tourists; most visitors rely on taxis, Didi, or a hired driver, which is required for travel outside Lhasa within the Tibet Autonomous Region.

train: Qinghai-Tibet Railway to Xining, Beijing, Chengdu and other mainland cities — one of the world's highest railways
bus: Long-distance sleeper buses to Golmud and other regional hubs

car.idp: Not recommended - independent foreign self-driving is heavily restricted

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in China and can even confuse or embarrass service staff; tour guides and drivers in Tibet are a common exception where a modest tip is appreciated.

food.name: Momo (Tibetan Dumplings)
food.desc: Steamed or pan-fried dumplings stuffed with minced yak, onion and coriander, eaten with chilli sauce and a bowl of broth.

places.name: Tibetan Family Kitchen
places.note: Home kitchen off the Barkhor circuit famous for momo and hands-on cooking classes.

places.name: Lhasa Kitchen
places.note: Long-running traveller favourite with reliably good yak momo and English menus.

places.name: Crazy Yak Saloon
places.note: Tibetan-decorated dining room with nightly song and dance alongside classic momo plates.

food.name: Thukpa (Tibetan Noodle Soup)
food.desc: Hand-pulled noodles in a clear yak-bone broth with radish, greens and meat; the everyday warming meal at 3,650 metres.

places.name: Pentoc Tibetan Restaurant
places.note: Homemade Tibetan cooking, with thukpa and shemdre the dishes regulars order.

places.name: Tashi I
places.note: Decades-old Lhasa institution near the Kirey Hotel serving thukpa, momo and tsampa.

places.name: Snowland Restaurant
places.note: Established restaurant close to Jokhang Temple with a broad Tibetan and Nepali menu.

food.name: Tsampa (Roasted Barley Flour)
food.desc: Highland barley toasted and milled, then kneaded by hand with butter tea into a dough ball; the staple food of the Tibetan plateau.

places.name: Tibetan Family Kitchen
places.note: Shows visitors how to knead tsampa properly as part of its family-style meals.

places.name: Tashi I
places.note: One of the easiest places for newcomers to try tsampa with an explanation in English.

places.name: Guangming Gangqiong Sweet Tea House
places.note: Vast local tea hall where tsampa is eaten with bottomless tea by Lhasa residents.

food.name: Yak Meat, Stir-Fried and Air-Dried
food.desc: Yak beef stir-fried with chilli and potato, or hung to air-dry into chewy jerky eaten as a snack through the winter.

places.name: Crazy Yak Saloon
places.note: Named for the dish; strong reputation for its yak steaks and stir-fries.

places.name: Makye Ame
places.note: Famous yellow building on the Barkhor kora with Tibetan and Nepali yak dishes.

places.name: Lhasa Kitchen
places.note: Dependable yak curries, ribs and stir-fries in the old-town restaurant strip.

food.name: Shemdre (Yak and Potato over Rice)
food.desc: Comforting Tibetan plate of rice topped with yak meat and potato simmered in a mild, lightly spiced gravy.

places.name: Pentoc Tibetan Restaurant
places.note: Homemade shemdre is a house speciality alongside momo and butter tea.

places.name: Tibetan Family Kitchen
places.note: Family recipes including shemdre and sweet rice, cooked to order in small batches.

places.name: Snowland Restaurant
places.note: Reliable old-town kitchen serving the full range of Tibetan rice plates.

food.name: Droma Dresi (Sweet Rice with Ginseng Root)
food.desc: Festive sweet rice cooked with butter, sugar and tiny droma roots dug from the plateau; served at Losar and celebrations.

places.name: Tibetan Family Kitchen
places.note: One of the few kitchens that cooks sweet rice for visitors on request.

places.name: Makye Ame
places.note: Tourist-friendly Barkhor landmark that keeps traditional sweet dishes on the menu.

places.name: Guangming Gangqiong Sweet Tea House
places.note: Sweet rice and yoghurt sold cheaply alongside the endless pots of tea.

food.name: Po Cha (Yak Butter Tea)
food.desc: Brick tea churned with yak butter and salt into a savoury, soupy brew; drunk all day and the liquid that tsampa is mixed with.

places.name: Guangming Gangqiong Sweet Tea House
places.note: Lhasa's best-known tea hall, packed with pilgrims and locals from dawn.

places.name: Tibetan Family Kitchen
places.note: Churns butter tea the traditional way and explains the ritual to guests.

places.name: Pentoc Tibetan Restaurant
places.note: Serves butter tea by the pot with its homemade Tibetan meals.

food.name: Cha Ngarmo (Tibetan Sweet Milk Tea)
food.desc: Black tea boiled with milk and sugar, poured from thermoses by the glass; the social drink of Lhasa's tea houses.

places.name: Guangming Gangqiong Sweet Tea House
places.note: Pay by the jug and sit elbow to elbow with locals; a genuine Lhasa ritual.

places.name: Jiri Sweet Tea House
places.note: Popular neighbourhood tea house serving sweet tea with Tibetan noodles.

places.name: Tashi I
places.note: Easy first stop for sweet tea if the busy local tea halls feel daunting.

landmarks: Potala Palace
The Dalai Lamas' towering 17th-century winter palace climbs Red Hill in a thousand-room cascade of white and crimson walls, crowning Lhasa as Tibet's defining UNESCO icon.
Jokhang Temple
Tibet's holiest shrine draws prostrating pilgrims from across the plateau to its golden-roofed 7th-century halls, home of the revered Jowo Shakyamuni Buddha statue.
Barkhor Street
This ancient circumambulation circuit ringing the Jokhang swirls with pilgrims spinning prayer wheels past incense burners, market stalls, and centuries-old whitewashed Tibetan townhouses.
Sera Monastery
Famous for its lively afternoon debates, where red-robed monks clap and lunge to punctuate philosophical points, this 15th-century Gelugpa monastery sprawls beneath a rocky hillside.
Drepung Monastery
Once the world's largest monastery housing 10,000 monks, this vast whitewashed complex tumbles down Mount Gephel and hosts the giant thangka unveiling during Shoton Festival.
Norbulingka (Jewel Park)
The Dalai Lamas' UNESCO-listed summer palace spreads through Lhasa's largest garden, its pavilions and murals offering a gentler, greener counterpoint to the Potala's grandeur.
Ramoche Temple
Lhasa's second-holiest temple, founded in the 7th century by Princess Wencheng's era, shelters a precious statue of the young Shakyamuni amid butter-lamp-lit chapels.
Chakpori Hill
This sacred hill opposite the Potala delivers the classic postcard panorama of the palace at sunrise, with prayer flags fluttering above thousands of carved mani stones.
Ganden Monastery
A dramatic day trip from Lhasa, the mother monastery of the Gelugpa order rings a 4,300-meter ridge with chapels and a breathtaking kora path over the Kyichu Valley.
Yamdrok Lake (Yamdrok Yumtso)
One of Tibet's three great sacred lakes shimmers turquoise beneath snow peaks a few hours from Lhasa, its scorpion-shaped waters an unforgettable high-altitude excursion.

train.note: No international trains reach Lhasa; the Qinghai-Tibet railway is entirely domestic and stops at the Tibetan plateau. Direct services run from Beijing West (daily, about 44 hours), Shanghai (daily, about 48 hours), Guangzhou (every other day, about 55 hours), Chengdu and Chongqing (every other day, 44-45 hours), Lanzhou (daily, about 27 hours) and Xining West (daily, about 24 hours), all crossing the Tanggula pass at over 5,000 m with piped oxygen in the carriages. Foreign visitors cannot buy Tibet train tickets without a Tibet Travel Permit, which your tour agency arranges and physically delivers, and your passport and permit are checked at a control point immediately outside Lhasa station where your guide is expected to meet you. The slow ascent by rail is genuinely better for acclimatisation than flying in.

bus.note: There are no scheduled international coaches, and non-Chinese nationals are in any case barred from using intercity buses anywhere in Tibet - Chinese nationals have frequent cheap services from Lhasa to nearly every part of the region. Foreign travellers must move around Tibet in a chartered vehicle with a licensed guide, booked as part of the permit package. The overland route to Kathmandu via the Gyirong (Kerung) crossing is done the same way, as a multi-day agency-arranged 4WD trip rather than a public bus, and it requires a Nepalese visa plus a separate Chinese group visa if you intend to return.

ferry.note: Lhasa lies on the Tibetan plateau at around 3,650 m, some 2,000 km from the sea, and the Lhasa River is shallow and unnavigable - there are no passenger ferry services.

half.name: Drak Yerpa
half.blurb: Meditation caves in cliffs northeast of Lhasa, built up since the 7th century as a retreat site tied to Tibetan Buddhism's early history.

half.name: Tsurphu Monastery
half.blurb: The seat of the Karmapa lineage in a valley about 70 kilometers from Lhasa, rebuilt after damage during the Cultural Revolution.

full.name: Namtso Lake
full.blurb: One of the world's highest lakes at 4,718 meters, roughly 240 kilometers from Lhasa across the Nyenchen Tanglha mountains.

full.name: Samye Monastery
full.blurb: Tibet's first Buddhist monastery, built in the 8th century in the Yarlung Valley and reached from Lhasa by road and a river crossing.
